prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one prize part, B027, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case is the discovery and its change of the field. Holst established GLP-1 secretion and action in humans, Drucker established the biology and the therapeutic concept, and Mojsov identified and synthesised the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide. Together they define the incretin mechanism, which more than two decades of independent work and randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease have confirmed. The first round did not weaken the scientific case or its maturity; no member contests either. The chair's central question is whether the citation honours the physiology and active peptide or the physiology-to-medicine arc including analogue design. I answer the first: the prize rewards the discovery that made the therapy possible, and the citation wording says so. A single part keeps the credit clean and uses no more than three names.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point, and round 1 did not resolve it. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener cannot be settled from the supplied material, and I have only recollection and the credited list, not documents. If the committee concluded that her contribution was derivative or not independent, my third name would fall and the cleaner fallback would be Drucker and Holst alone, not an unsupported substitution. Linnarsson and Wahren-Herlenius also make a fair point that a physiology prize may be read as honouring the hormone while leaving out the drug patients take, and that Knudsen's acylated analogues are the step that made GLP-1 usable. I think that is an industrial application of established knowledge, but it is a judgement about what the prize rewards, not a fact I can prove.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds that Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is the right trio, because solving the half-life problem with acylated analogues was itself a discovery and the step that took GLP-1 from physiology to patients.
responses.response: I have reconsidered this and I do not change my view, though I think your argument is the strongest on the other side. Designing an albumin-binding, DPP-4-resistant analogue is inventive medicinal chemistry, but it works because the peptide, its glucose-dependent action and its receptor were already defined by the three discovery-side laureates. The prize recognises the discovery that enabled the therapy. You also say you would accept Mojsov if the citation is about the hormone and not the drug. I propose exactly that, so on your own condition the disagreement narrows to whether the priority record is firm enough. On that point we agree that it is the open question. We differ on the fallback: if it fails I would go to a two-name Drucker and Holst prize, not substitute Knudsen, because that would change what the prize honours as a way of avoiding the dispute.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would accept Knudsen as a defensible substitute for Mojsov only if the priority dispute over the peptide cannot be resolved, and ranks CAR-T and TNF blockade as alternatives to GLP-1.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning that the enabling step is the identification of the active peptide and its insulinotropic action, and that drug engineering builds on it. I disagree with substituting Knudsen if the priority question stays open. An unresolved dispute between Mojsov and Habener is a question about who identified the peptide, and replacing her with a name from the next stage does not answer it, it moves the prize to a different achievement. If the record cannot support Mojsov, I think the more defensible result is two names. On your alternatives, I still rank CAR-T below B014 and B010 because Eshhar's chimeric receptor work is outside the credited names, as you note, so I do not see a clean three-name credit there. The decisive point for B027 is that the evidence sits with the committee, not with any one of us, and that it should be checked before the vote.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, holds that tool status is no demerit for optogenetics and that B014 is the safer second prize if the committee wants a pair without disputed credit.
responses.response: I accept your correction that I may have treated tool status as too heavy a demerit. A method that opens causal dissection of circuits has precedent, and I will not hold it against B015. My remaining objection is attribution, not category: six credited names, a disputed priority among Boyden, Deisseroth and Miesenbock, and a channelrhodopsin discovery that is separable from its neuronal use. I agree with you that B014 is the cleaner pair. On the chair's question whether a second part should be considered at all, I say no. Every member proposes one part, no second candidate has a settled credit, and adding a part would put pressure on the names for B027. Of the alternatives I would keep B014 ahead of B015 only because Walter and Mori need no exclusion.

responses.point: El-Manira argues that being a tool does not lower optogenetics and that it ranks above the unfolded protein response for breadth, while accepting that B014 has the cleaner attribution.
responses.response: I take the point that breadth of use across excitable-cell physiology is a real argument and that the prize has recognised methods. We still cannot settle the trio: your Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth and my Bamberg, Deisseroth and Nagel differ on one place, and the committee would have to leave out someone it considers essential. That is why I keep the unfolded protein response as my first alternative. I agree with your earlier suggestion, which I shared, that the committee ask for the documentary record on Mojsov before the vote and not decide from memory. I do not move B015 into my alternatives, although I now hold that view with less certainty than in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification and synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) is independent and prior enough to be credited, and how Habener's work bears on it; I cannot decide this from the supplied material.
If the record is unclear, I would move to a two-name Drucker and Holst prize, but I do not know who decides that or when, and a reasonable member could prefer a different fallback.
Whether the committee wants the citation to honour physiology and the active peptide or the arc through analogue design; my wording follows the first answer and a majority could choose the second.
Whether optogenetics can be reduced to three names without an injustice, which affects how it ranks against B014 as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the credited GLP-1 laureates or my alternatives B014 and B010. My documented work on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not overlap with them. My profile notes about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson, who also lists B014 as an alternative, and one with Abdel El Manira; neither concerns any credited candidate. I infer no personal ties from shared institutions. The profile does not establish the voting status of the Secretary-General, and I take part here on the basis that all six members vote.
